'''''Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose''''' is an [[oil-on-canvas]] painting made by the American painter [[John Singer Sargent]] in 1885–86.<ref name="Tate">{{cite web | url=http://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/sargent-carnation-lily-lily-rose-n01615 | title=Tate Gallery | accessdate=February 5, 2013}}</ref>

The painting depicts two small children dressed in white who are lighting [[paper lantern]]s as day turns to evening; they are in a garden strewn with pink roses, accents of yellow carnations and tall white [[lily|lilies]] (possibly the Japanese mountain lily, ''[[Lilium auratum]]'') behind them.
The painting is dominated by green foliage, with no horizon or other horizontal line to give a sense of depth. The viewer seems to be on a level with the children but also looking down on them.  
The two subjects of the painting are the daughters of the illustrator [[Fred Barnard|Frederick Barnard]], a friend of Sargent's. Dolly, left, was 11 years old and Polly, right, seven years old; they were chosen for their blonde hair, replacing Sargent's original model, [[Francis Davis Millet]]'s five-year-old daughter, dark-haired Katherine.<ref name="TateCatalogue">{{cite web|title=Catalogue entry: 'Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose', John Singer Sargent, 1885–6|url=http://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/sargent-carnation-lily-lily-rose-n01615/text-catalogue-entry|website=Tate|accessdate=31 May 2017}}</ref>
The title comes from the refrain of a popular song "Ye Shepherds Tell Me" by [[Joseph Mazzinghi]], a pastoral glee for a trio of male voices, which mentions Flora wearing "A wreath around her head, around her head she wore, Carnation, lily, lily, rose".<ref>{{cite web|title="Ye Shepherds Tell Me" by Joseph Mazzinghi|url=http://www.jssgallery.org/Letters/Notes/Carnation_Lilly/Ye_Shepherds.html|website=John Singer Sargent Virtual Gallery|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130603010947/http://www.jssgallery.org/Letters/Notes/Carnation_Lilly/Ye_Shepherds.html|archivedate=3 June 2013}}</ref>

The work is set in an English garden at Farnham House in [[Broadway, Worcestershire|Broadway]] in the [[Cotswolds]], where Sargent spent the summer of 1885 with Millet shortly after moving to England from Paris to escape the scandal caused by his 1884 painting ''[[Portrait of Madame X]]''. The author [[Robert Louis Stevenson]] was also staying there while writing ''[[A Child's Garden of Verses]]'' and his verses inspired Sargent.
Sargent also took inspiration from the lanterns that he saw hanging among trees and lilies while boating on the [[River Thames]] at [[Pangbourne]] with American artist [[Edwin Austin Abbey]] in September 1885.
Sargent wanted to capture the exact level of light at dusk so he painted the picture ''[[en plein air]]'' – outdoors and in the [[Impressionist]] manner.
Every day from September to November 1885, he painted in the few minutes when the light was perfect, giving the picture an overall [[Blue hour|purple tint]] of evening.<ref name="TateCatalogue" />
The flowers in the garden died as summer turned to autumn, and they were replaced with artificial flowers.
Sargent resumed painting the following summer at Millet's new home nearby in Broadway and finally finished the painting by the end of October 1886.  
In the course of working, Sargent cut down the rectangular canvas, removing approximately {{convert|2|ft|cm}} from the left side, to leave an approximately square shape.<ref name="TateCatalogue" />

The work received a mixed reception at the [[Royal Academy summer exhibition]] in 1887, with some criticising his "Frenchified" style. However, there was also much praise, and Sir [[Frederic Leighton]], President of the Royal Academy, encouraged the [[Tate Gallery]] to buy the painting later that year, using money from the [[Chantrey Bequest]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Simpson|first1=Marc|last2=Sargent|first2=John Singer|last3=Ormond|first3=Richard|last4=Weinberg|first4=Helene Barbara|last5=Institute|first5=Sterling and Francine Clark Art|title=Uncanny Spectacle: The Public Career of the Young John Singer Sargent|date=January 1997|publisher=Yale University Press|isbn=0300071779|page=155|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-nFsM8EMjQEC&pg=PA155|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose, John Singer Sargent, 1885–6|url=http://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/sargent-carnation-lily-lily-rose-n01615/text-summary|website=Tate|accessdate=31 May 2017}}</ref> It was the first of Sargent's works to be acquired by a public museum. The painting remains part of the Tate collection and is displayed at [[Tate Britain]].
